reviews.strategic-interaction-and-game-theory: Game theory turns interactions into strategies and payoffs, drawn as tables or trees, and the Nash equilibrium marks where no one gains by changing alone, even when everyone could be better off. Different games capture different troubles: the prisoner's dilemma makes cooperation hard, Chicken makes conflict likely, and the stag hunt shows that the best joint outcome may simply need trust. Repetition changes the picture, because strategies such as tit for tat and the threat of punishment can sustain cooperation among patient players, as the folk theorem shows. Evolutionary game theory carries the same logic into nature, from hawk–dove contests to the reciprocal altruism of guppies inspecting predators. Cooperative game theory, bargaining and auctions ask the final question: how to divide what players can only create together.

nature-econ-715.title: Perfect and imperfect information: who saw what
nature-econ-715.text: In some games every player always knows everything that has happened so far. Those games have perfect information. If some earlier move is hidden, because moves are simultaneous or simply unobserved, the game has imperfect information. On a game tree, the decision points a player cannot tell apart are joined by a dotted line or a loop, forming an {{ref:nature-econ-679}}. Any game in which such a set contains more than one decision point has imperfect information.

nature-econ-716.title: The Harsanyi transformation: letting Nature choose the types
nature-econ-716.text: What if players do not know each other's payoffs or types? The Harsanyi transformation adds Nature as a player who chooses the types at the start. A game of incomplete information then becomes one of complete but imperfect information. For example, Nature might pick a job applicant's ability as low with probability 1/3 or high with probability 2/3, and the employer does not see the pick. Nature has no payoffs, and its choice is drawn as an unfilled node.

nature-econ-677.title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium: best play given beliefs
nature-econ-677.text: In a Bayesian game, players do not know each other's types. A Bayesian Nash equilibrium is that game's Nash equilibrium. Each player's strategy maximizes their expected payoff, given their beliefs about others' types and the others' strategies. Players form those beliefs about the unknown state of nature using Bayes' rule, a formula for updating probabilities with new evidence. In dynamic games where players move in turn, it can produce implausible equilibria based on non-credible strategies or beliefs. It also matters in designing rules and institutions: if everyone's best play is to report their true preferences, the mechanism is called incentive compatible.

nature-econ-679.title: Information sets: not knowing where you stand
nature-econ-679.text: Sometimes a player must move without knowing exactly what has happened. An information set is the group of that player's decision points that they cannot tell apart, so they do not know which one they are at. In game trees, information sets are usually drawn with dotted lines. Chance moves are made by 'Nature', usually shown as an unfilled circle at the root of the tree.

nature-econ-733.title: Behavior strategies: randomizing step by step
nature-econ-733.text: A mixed strategy randomly picks a fixed path through the game tree. A behavior strategy instead takes a random path, randomizing separately at each information set over the actions available there. Kuhn's theorem shows the two are equivalent in finite extensive-form games with perfect recall, where players remember all past actions. The Absent-Minded Driver game shows why perfect recall is needed for this equivalence.

nature-econ-678.title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium: consistent beliefs, optimal moves
nature-econ-678.text: Games with both hidden information and moves in sequence need a sharper tool. A perfect Bayesian equilibrium requires two things. Players' beliefs must be consistent with the strategies being played, and every player must choose optimally given those beliefs. Like subgame perfect equilibrium, it demands optimal play from every information set onward. That rules out non-credible threats and beliefs.

nature-econ-739.title: Generous tit for tat: forgiving now and then
nature-econ-739.text: Tit for tat has a weak spot: one misread move can set off endless retaliation. Generous tit for tat repairs it. After the opponent defects, it usually retaliates but sometimes cooperates anyway, with a small probability. That occasional forgiveness breaks cycles of retaliation caused by mistakes or 'noise', and restores mutual cooperation. Axelrod found it highly effective in noisy settings, with a forgiveness probability around 1–5%, depending on the opponents.

nature-econ-740.title: Reciprocal altruism: favors returned in nature
nature-econ-740.text: Guppies cooperate to inspect predators, and tit for tat has been suggested as the mechanism behind it. That is reciprocal altruism: helping another animal in the expectation that the favour will be returned when needs reverse. It works where the cost to the helper of sharing food, mates, nests or territory is less than the gain to the one helped. It stays stable because animals have ways of spotting and punishing 'cheaters' who fail to return favours, which in effect is tit for tat.

nature-econ-738.title: Tit for two tats: letting one betrayal slide
nature-econ-738.text: Tit for two tats is a more forgiving cousin of tit for tat: it retaliates only after the opponent defects twice in a row. Letting a single defection pass avoids the 'death spiral' of two retaliators punishing each other forever. Robert Axelrod found it would have outscored every program in his first tournament. It has a modern use too. BitTorrent file-sharing peers use a variant of it to swap upload for download bandwidth.

nature-econ-709.title: The bourgeois strategy: let ownership decide
nature-econ-709.text: A bourgeois strategy settles contests by using some asymmetry between the rivals, such as who already holds the resource. In the hawk–dove game, treating one player as territory owner and the other as intruder makes such role-based strategies stable. When an asymmetry like this exists, the bourgeois strategy can also beat a bluffing strategy in the war of attrition.

nature-econ-712.title: Coevolutionary games: species shaping species
nature-econ-712.text: Predator and prey, host and parasite, and partners in {{ref:nature-eco-366}} all evolve in response to one another. Coevolutionary games model this by combining competition within a species with competition between species. They add a third kind of dynamic, beyond games that settle at a stable strategy and games that cycle.

nature-econ-710.title: How can altruism evolve?
nature-econ-710.text: Darwin noticed a puzzle. If selection acts only on individuals, behavior that helps another at a cost to oneself makes no sense, yet many social animals behave altruistically. Game theory offers several routes out. Kin selection works through shared genes: Hamilton's rule says relatedness must exceed the ratio of cost to benefit. Direct reciprocity ('I'll scratch your back if you scratch mine') and indirect reciprocity are further routes. Without some measure of reputation, only direct reciprocity can arise in the prisoner's dilemma. Nowak and Wilson's group-selection explanation of insect colonies challenges the kin-selection account, and it is described as controversial.

nature-econ-711.title: Rock, paper, scissors in nature
nature-econ-711.text: Male side-blotched lizards come in three throat-colour types, each with its own mating strategy. Each type beats one rival and loses to the other, like rock, paper and scissors. In such games the strategies' shares cycle instead of settling down. Together with density effects in females, the lizards' contest drives a four-year population cycle. The cyclic behavior predicted by evolutionary game theory has also been seen in human laboratory experiments.

nature-econ-713.title: Spatial games: contests between neighbours
nature-econ-713.text: Spatial games are evolutionary game models that place players on a grid, so each contest is only with immediate neighbours. That small change makes location matter. Winning strategies take over local neighbourhoods first, and then spread into adjacent ones.

nature-econ-695.title: The characteristic function: what each coalition can earn
nature-econ-695.text: A cooperative game can be specified with a single list: a value for every possible coalition of players, with the empty coalition worth zero. That list is the characteristic function, the total payoff each coalition can secure by joining together. Characteristic functions are often assumed superadditive: two separate coalitions together are worth at least the sum of their separate values. In a simple game, every coalition is either winning, worth 1, or losing, worth 0.

nature-econ-706.title: The core: deals no group wants to walk away from
nature-econ-706.text: In a game of 1000 left-shoe owners and 1001 right-shoe owners, the core hands the scarce left-shoe owners everything and the right-shoe owners nothing. The core, in a cooperative game, is the set of allocations from which no group of players could do better by breaking away. A coalition blocks an allocation if its members could create more value on their own than they are given. The core therefore marks situations where cooperation among all players can be kept going. The idea appeared in Edgeworth's 1881 writing as the contract curve; the modern definition is due to Donald B. Gillies and Lloyd Shapley. The core is always well defined but can be empty. The Bondareva–Shapley theorem says it is non-empty exactly when the game is 'balanced'. Every Walrasian, or competitive market, equilibrium lies in the core, though not every core allocation is a market equilibrium. Critics point to the shoe example: the core is extremely sensitive to an oversupply of one type of player.

nature-econ-726.title: The Shapley value: a fair share of joint gains
nature-econ-726.text: How should a group divide the gains of working together? In 1951 Lloyd Shapley proposed an answer. The Shapley value looks at how much the result changes when a player joins every possible combination of others, then averages those changes. Each member's share is their average contribution. It is the only division that satisfies efficiency, symmetry, additivity and the null-player property, which are widely accepted as defining fairness. Efficiency means all the group's gain is shared out, and a player who adds nothing to any coalition gets zero. If cooperation creates positive synergy, every member gains at least what they could get alone. The method is used to divide business profits, and to measure each feature's importance in machine-learning models and in {{ref:nature-econ-273}}.

nature-econ-699.title: Convex cooperative games: coalitions that snowball
nature-econ-699.text: In some cooperative games, gains snowball: a newcomer adds more to a coalition the bigger it already is. Shapley introduced these convex games in 1971; formally, their characteristic function is supermodular. Convex games are totally balanced, meaning their core, and the core of every subgame, is non-empty. Similar results for submodular functions appear in combinatorial optimization.

nature-econ-698.title: The Harsanyi dividend: what a coalition adds
nature-econ-698.text: The Harsanyi dividend is the extra surplus a coalition creates beyond what its smaller sub-coalitions already create. It isolates the value that appears only when that exact group comes together. John Harsanyi used it in 1963 to generalize the Shapley value.

nature-econ-697.title: The nucleolus: shrinking the loudest complaint
nature-econ-697.text: Any allocation in a cooperative game can leave coalitions with a complaint, measured by what each could gain by leaving. The nucleolus is the allocation that makes the largest of these complaints as small as possible. It is always unique. And if the core is non-empty, the nucleolus lies inside it.

nature-econ-696.title: Stable sets: the first answer for many-player coalitions
nature-econ-696.text: Von Neumann and Morgenstern proposed the stable set, the first solution concept for cooperative games with more than two players. It is built on which allocations a coalition would object to. One allocation dominates another if some coalition prefers it and could obtain at least its members' payoffs on its own. Stable sets proved awkward. One may not exist, is usually not unique and is hard to find, which spurred the development of other solution concepts. The core is contained in every stable set.

nature-econ-727.title: The Aumann–Shapley value: fair shares for a vast crowd
nature-econ-727.text: The Aumann–Shapley value extends the Shapley value to games with a continuum of players, each of whom plays only a tiny role. Lloyd Shapley and Robert Aumann created it in their 1974 book, and Jean-François Mertens and Abraham Neyman extended it further.

nature-econ-701.title: Battle of the sexes: agreeing to meet, disagreeing on where
nature-econ-701.text: A couple argues over what to do at the weekend. Both would rather do the same thing than go alone, but each prefers a different plan. This battle of the sexes is a coordination game with conflicting interests. A round of {{ref:nature-val-075}} before play can help. It may let the players pick one of the game's several equilibria and earn more than without communication.

nature-econ-736.title: Credible threats: would you really do it?
nature-econ-736.text: A credible threat is one a player would actually want to carry out if the time came. A non-credible threat is one that would hurt the player making it. Plain Nash equilibrium can rest on threats players would never carry out, and subgame perfection eliminates them. In Chicken, a player who rips out their steering wheel always wins, because the opponent's threat to crash anyway is not credible. Punishment works the same way: if punishing a deviator is costly to the punishers, the threat of punishment is not credible.

nature-econ-684.title: Brinkmanship: the deliberate risk of losing control
nature-econ-684.text: Brinkmanship is a strategic move that deters an opponent from turning aggressive by credibly threatening a risk of irrational retaliation. The threat works only if the opponent believes there is enough risk of an irrational response. Often that belief arises because the threatener has given up control over the response. In everyday talk of conflict, 'chicken' and 'brinkmanship' are often used as synonyms.

nature-econ-682.title: Pre-commitment: winning by tying your own hands
nature-econ-682.text: A protester who handcuffs themselves to an object cannot be moved by any threat. That is pre-commitment: convincingly locking in one's own choice before a game starts, so that the other player must give way. In Chicken, a driver who visibly disables their steering wheel forces the other to swerve. Cutting one's own options, it turns out, can pay.
